chapters.title: Solomon asks for wisdom

parts.text: Solomon’s kingdom is strengthened because God is with him. He leads Israel’s assembly to Gibeon, where the tabernacle and brass altar stand, and offers a thousand burnt offerings. When God invites him to ask for a gift, Solomon requests wisdom and knowledge to govern God’s numerous people. Because he seeks this rather than wealth, honor, revenge, or long life, God grants wisdom and promises unmatched riches and honor as well.

Solomon returns to Jerusalem and rules Israel. The account describes his chariots, horsemen, abundant silver and gold, and trade in horses and chariots from Egypt. His wealth and military resources grow alongside his royal authority.

chapters.title: Solomon obtains help for the temple

parts.text: Solomon prepares to build the temple and his royal house. He organizes a large workforce and asks Huram of Tyre for timber and a skilled craftsman. He explains the regular worship intended for the temple while acknowledging that even the heavens cannot contain God. He offers wheat, barley, wine, and oil for the workers who will cut the timber.

Huram praises the Creator for giving David a wise son and sends an experienced craftsman able to work in many materials. He agrees to float timber by sea to Joppa for transport to Jerusalem. Solomon numbers the resident strangers and assigns them to carrying burdens, cutting stone, and overseeing the work.

chapters.title: The temple is built on mount Moriah

parts.text: Solomon begins building the LORD’s house in Jerusalem on mount Moriah, at the threshingfloor David prepared. The work starts in the fourth year of his reign. The temple’s dimensions, porch, gold coverings, precious stones, and carved decorations are described. The most holy place is richly overlaid with gold.

Two large gold-covered cherubims stand in the most holy place, their spread wings reaching across the room. A colored linen veil bears worked cherubims. Two pillars are set before the temple, adorned with chains and pomegranates. Solomon names the right-hand pillar Jachin and the left-hand pillar Boaz.

chapters.title: The temple furnishings

parts.text: Solomon makes the brass altar and a great basin called the sea, supported by twelve oxen. The sea is for the priests to wash in, while ten smaller lavers serve for washing what is offered as burnt offerings. Gold candlesticks, tables, and basins are arranged within the temple, and the courts and their doors are completed.

Huram finishes the brass work, including pillars, decorative pomegranates, bases, vessels, and utensils. The castings are made in the plain of Jordan, and the quantity of brass is too great to weigh. Gold furnishings and instruments, including the altar, lamps, and doors of the inner rooms, complete the house.

chapters.title: The ark enters the temple and God’s glory fills it

parts.text: With the temple finished, Solomon brings in the things David dedicated and gathers Israel’s elders and tribal heads. During the seventh-month feast, priests and Levites carry the ark and sacred vessels into the temple. Amid countless sacrifices, the ark is placed beneath the cherubims in the most holy place. It contains the two tables Moses placed there at Horeb.

The sanctified priests and Levitical singers unite in thanksgiving with trumpets and other instruments. They praise the LORD’s goodness and enduring mercy. A cloud fills the house, and the priests cannot stand to minister because the glory of the LORD has filled the temple.

chapters.title: Solomon prays for those who seek God

parts.text: Solomon blesses Israel and praises God for fulfilling the promise that David’s son would build the temple. Kneeling before the assembly, he asks God to maintain the covenant and hear prayer directed toward this place. He acknowledges that heaven itself cannot contain God, much less the house he has built, and asks God to hear from heaven and forgive.

His prayer covers disputes, defeat, drought, famine, sickness, warfare, and captivity. When people confess and return to God, he asks for forgiveness and help, according to the hearts God alone knows. He also asks God to hear foreigners who come because of his name, so all peoples may know and fear him. He closes by appealing for God’s presence and favor.

chapters.title: The dedication and God’s answer

parts.text: When Solomon finishes praying, fire comes from heaven and consumes the sacrifices, and God’s glory fills the temple. The people bow in worship and praise his enduring mercy. Abundant offerings accompany the dedication, and the assembled nation keeps the feast. The people return home rejoicing in God’s goodness to David, Solomon, and Israel.

God appears to Solomon and accepts the temple as a house of sacrifice. If his people humble themselves, pray, seek him, and turn from wickedness, he will hear, forgive, and heal their land. He promises to establish Solomon’s throne if he obeys, but warns that forsaking God for idols will bring removal from the land and the temple’s rejection.

chapters.title: Solomon’s building, worship, and trade

parts.text: Solomon strengthens and settles cities throughout his territory after completing the temple and palace. He builds fortified towns, store cities, and places for his chariots and horsemen. Remaining non-Israelite peoples pay tribute, while Israelites serve as soldiers and officers. Pharaoh’s daughter moves into a separate house because Solomon regards the places associated with the ark as holy.

Sacrifices are offered according to Moses’ commandments at the appointed daily, weekly, and yearly times. Priests, Levites, and gatekeepers serve in the divisions David established. The temple work is completed. With ships and experienced sailors supplied by Huram, Solomon’s servants travel to Ophir and bring back gold.

chapters.title: The queen of Sheba and Solomon’s glory

parts.text: The queen of Sheba comes to test Solomon with hard questions and brings rich gifts. He answers everything she asks. Seeing his wisdom, household, and worship, she declares that the report she heard did not tell half his greatness. She praises God for placing him over Israel to exercise justice. Solomon gives her what she desires before she returns home.

The chapter describes Solomon’s immense revenues, gold shields, ivory-and-gold throne, splendid vessels, fleets, horses, and dominion. Other rulers seek his God-given wisdom and bring presents. After reigning forty years, Solomon dies and is buried in David’s city. His son Rehoboam becomes king.

chapters.title: Rehoboam’s harsh answer divides the kingdom

parts.text: Israel gathers at Shechem to make Rehoboam king. Jeroboam returns from Egypt, and the people ask for relief from Solomon’s heavy demands. Rehoboam seeks advice: the older counselors urge kindness and a favorable answer, while his young companions recommend threatening an even heavier burden. He rejects the elders’ counsel.

When the people return, Rehoboam answers harshly and promises greater oppression. The account says this turn fulfills the LORD’s word through Ahijah. Israel rejects David’s house, though Rehoboam retains the people in Judah’s cities. Hadoram, the officer over tribute, is stoned to death, and Rehoboam escapes to Jerusalem. The division becomes an enduring rebellion.

chapters.title: Rehoboam strengthens Judah

parts.text: Rehoboam assembles Judah and Benjamin to recover the northern kingdom by force. Through Shemaiah, the LORD forbids them to fight their brethren, declaring that the division is from him. They obey and return home. Rehoboam then fortifies cities throughout Judah and Benjamin, supplying them with commanders, food, shields, and spears.

Priests and Levites leave their possessions in the north after Jeroboam excludes them from the LORD’s service. Others who seek God follow them to Jerusalem, strengthening Judah during three years of faithfulness. Rehoboam’s wives and children are described. He favors Maachah, appoints her son Abijah as the intended successor, and distributes his sons among fortified cities.

chapters.title: Shishak invades after Judah forsakes the law

parts.text: Once established, Rehoboam and his people forsake the LORD’s law. Shishak of Egypt invades, captures fortified cities, and advances to Jerusalem. Shemaiah declares that God has left them in Shishak’s hands because they forsook him. The king and leaders humble themselves and acknowledge God’s righteousness. God grants partial deliverance, but they must serve Shishak and learn the difference between his service and foreign rule.

Shishak takes the temple and palace treasures, including Solomon’s gold shields, which Rehoboam replaces with brass. The account credits his humiliation with averting complete destruction, yet judges his reign evil because he did not set his heart to seek God. Abijah succeeds him.

chapters.title: Abijah’s appeal and Judah’s victory

parts.text: Abijah reigns over Judah and faces Jeroboam’s much larger army. He appeals to God’s enduring covenant with David and condemns Jeroboam’s rebellion, golden calves, and replacement priesthood. He contrasts this with Judah’s service through Aaron’s priests and the Levites, warning Israel that fighting them means opposing the LORD.

Jeroboam sets an ambush behind Judah. Surrounded, Judah cries to God, the priests sound trumpets, and the army shouts. God defeats Israel, and Judah prevails because they rely on him. Abijah takes several towns. Jeroboam never regains strength during Abijah’s reign and is struck by the LORD, while Abijah grows powerful and his household increases.

chapters.title: Asa’s reforms and victory over Zerah

parts.text: After Abijah dies, Asa becomes king and the land has ten years of quiet. He removes foreign altars, images, and groves, and commands Judah to seek the LORD and obey his law. During the rest God gives them, the people build fortified cities. Asa also prepares an army from Judah and Benjamin.

Zerah the Ethiopian advances with a vast host. Asa cries to the LORD, acknowledging that God can help the powerless against the strong and declaring reliance upon him. God defeats the Ethiopians, and Judah pursues them to Gerar. They return with abundant spoil, sheep, and camels after overcoming the surrounding settlements.

chapters.title: A covenant to seek the LORD

parts.text: The Spirit of God moves Azariah to encourage Asa and his people. He declares that the LORD is with those who seek him but will forsake those who forsake him. He recalls times of disorder when Israel lacked God’s instruction, and how turning to God in trouble brought help. Asa is urged to continue courageously because his work will be rewarded.

Asa removes idols, repairs the altar, and gathers Judah with people who have come from northern tribes. They sacrifice and covenant wholeheartedly to seek God, imposing death for refusal. Asa removes Maachah from her royal position because of her idol. Although high places remain in Israel, his heart is described as perfect, and God gives rest.

chapters.title: Asa relies on Syria and rejects correction

parts.text: Baasha fortifies Ramah to restrict movement into Judah. Asa sends temple and palace treasures to Ben-hadad of Syria, asking him to break his alliance with Baasha. Syrian attacks force Baasha to abandon the work, and Asa uses its materials to build Geba and Mizpah.

Hanani rebukes Asa for relying on Syria rather than the LORD who had delivered him from the Ethiopians. He warns of future wars. Asa responds by imprisoning the seer and oppressing some of the people. Later, when severely diseased in his feet, he seeks physicians but not the LORD. He dies in his forty-first year and receives an honorable burial.

chapters.title: Jehoshaphat strengthens Judah and sends teachers

parts.text: Jehoshaphat succeeds Asa, fortifies Judah, and seeks the LORD rather than Baalim. God establishes his kingdom, and Judah brings him gifts. He removes high places and groves and sends princes, Levites, and priests through the cities with the book of the law to teach the people.

The fear of the LORD restrains surrounding kingdoms from making war. Philistines bring tribute, and Arabians bring flocks. Jehoshaphat grows powerful, building fortresses and store cities. The chapter names military commanders and their large companies from Judah and Benjamin, distinguishing them from the forces stationed in the fortified towns. His prosperity is joined to organized defense and instruction in God’s law.

chapters.title: Micaiah warns Ahab before the battle

parts.text: Jehoshaphat joins Ahab in a campaign against Ramoth-gilead but asks for God’s counsel. Four hundred prophets promise success. Micaiah, summoned despite Ahab’s hostility, reports Israel scattered like sheep without a shepherd. He describes a heavenly vision in which a lying spirit entices Ahab through his prophets. For this warning he is struck and imprisoned until Ahab returns safely, something Micaiah says will not happen if the LORD has spoken.

Ahab enters battle in disguise while Jehoshaphat wears royal robes. God helps Jehoshaphat escape mistaken pursuit. An arrow strikes Ahab between the joints of his armor, and he dies at sunset, fulfilling the warning he rejected.

chapters.title: Jehoshaphat appoints judges

parts.text: Jehoshaphat returns safely to Jerusalem, but Jehu the seer rebukes him for helping the ungodly and loving those who hate the LORD. He also acknowledges the king’s removal of groves and desire to seek God. Jehoshaphat goes among the people to bring them back to the LORD and appoints judges in the fortified cities, charging them to judge for God without partiality or bribery.

In Jerusalem he establishes Levites, priests, and family heads to resolve disputes and instruct the people against wrongdoing. Different leaders oversee matters of the LORD and of the king. The judges must act faithfully, courageously, and in the fear of God.

chapters.title: God delivers Judah without a battle

parts.text: Faced with an invading multitude, Jehoshaphat proclaims a fast and leads Judah in prayer. He recalls God’s promises and confesses that they lack both strength and knowledge of what to do. Through Jahaziel, God tells them not to fear: the battle is his. They must go out, stand, and see his salvation. The assembly bows in worship.

Singers lead the army in praise. God turns the enemies against one another, leaving Judah to gather abundant spoil. They return rejoicing, and surrounding kingdoms fear God. Jehoshaphat is judged faithful overall, though high places remain. His later shipping partnership with wicked Ahaziah is condemned, and the ships are wrecked before sailing.

chapters.title: Jehoram’s cruelty and downfall

parts.text: Jehoram succeeds Jehoshaphat and kills his brothers and some of Israel’s princes. Married into Ahab’s family, he follows its evil ways and leads Judah into unfaithfulness. Yet God preserves David’s house because of his covenant. Edom and Libnah revolt against Judah during Jehoram’s reign.

A writing from Elijah condemns Jehoram’s idolatry and the murder of brothers better than himself. It announces disaster upon his household and a grievous disease. Philistines and Arabians invade and carry away his possessions and family, leaving only his youngest son. God then strikes him with an incurable bowel disease. He dies without being desired and is buried apart from the kings’ tombs.

chapters.title: Ahaziah’s death and Joash’s preservation

parts.text: Ahaziah succeeds his father and follows the counsel of Athaliah and Ahab’s house. He joins Israel’s king against Syria and later visits the wounded Joram at Jezreel. His association brings him into Jehu’s judgment upon Ahab’s family. Jehu kills Judah’s princes and Ahaziah’s relatives, and Ahaziah is captured and killed. His household is left unable to retain the kingdom.

Athaliah responds to her son’s death by destroying the royal children and taking power. Jehoshabeath, Ahaziah’s sister and the wife of Jehoiada the priest, rescues the infant Joash with his nurse. He remains hidden in the house of God for six years while Athaliah rules.

chapters.title: Jehoiada restores the rightful king

parts.text: In the seventh year, Jehoiada gathers commanders, Levites, and family heads into a covenant to establish David’s heir. He arranges armed guards around the temple while preserving its rules of access. Joash is brought out, crowned, given the testimony, and anointed king amid cries for his welfare.

Athaliah hears the celebration, comes to the temple, and cries treason. Jehoiada orders her taken outside the sanctuary, where she is killed. He renews the covenant that king and people will belong to the LORD. They destroy Baal’s house and images, kill its priest, restore ordered temple service, and seat Joash on the throne. The people rejoice, and the city becomes quiet.

chapters.title: Joash repairs the temple, then turns away

parts.text: Joash does right while Jehoiada lives and undertakes to repair the temple. After delays in collecting funds, a chest is placed at the gate, and the people give gladly. Workmen restore the building, and remaining money supplies sacred vessels. Offerings continue throughout Jehoiada’s lifetime. When the priest dies at 130, he is buried among the kings because of the good he has done.

Afterward, Joash listens to Judah’s leaders, and they forsake the LORD for idols. He orders Jehoiada’s son Zechariah stoned for rebuking them. A small Syrian army then defeats Judah as judgment. Joash is left diseased and is killed by his servants, who avenge the blood of Jehoiada’s sons.

chapters.title: Amaziah’s victory becomes a snare

parts.text: Amaziah does right but not wholeheartedly. He executes his father’s murderers while sparing their children according to Moses’ law. Preparing for war, he hires Israelite soldiers but sends them home at a man of God’s warning, trusting God can replace the lost payment. Judah defeats Edom and kills its captives; the dismissed soldiers retaliate by raiding Judah’s towns.

Amaziah adopts the gods of conquered Edom and threatens the prophet who rebukes him. Proud of victory, he challenges Israel’s king Joash and ignores a warning against reckless war. Judah is defeated, Amaziah captured, Jerusalem’s wall breached, and its treasures taken. Later conspirators pursue Amaziah to Lachish and kill him.

chapters.title: Uzziah’s prosperity and presumptuous incense offering

parts.text: Uzziah becomes king at sixteen and prospers while he seeks God. He defeats neighboring enemies, receives tribute, strengthens Jerusalem’s walls, and develops farms, wells, and towers. His army is well equipped, including devices for firing arrows and large stones. His fame spreads because he is wonderfully helped until he becomes strong.

Strength leads to pride. Uzziah enters the temple to burn incense, a duty reserved for Aaron’s descendants. Azariah and eighty priests oppose him. While he angrily resists, leprosy appears on his forehead. He leaves hurriedly and remains a leper in a separate house until death, excluded from the LORD’s house, while his son Jotham governs.

chapters.title: Jotham orders his ways before God

parts.text: Jotham follows the good example of Uzziah but does not enter the temple as his father did. The people, however, continue in corruption. He builds the temple’s high gate, strengthens the wall of Ophel, and constructs cities, castles, and towers. He defeats the Ammonites, who pay substantial tribute for three years.

The account attributes Jotham’s growing power to his ordering his ways before the LORD. His wars and conduct are recorded in the royal history. After reigning sixteen years in Jerusalem, he dies and is buried in David’s city. His son Ahaz succeeds him.

chapters.title: Ahaz’s idolatry and Judah’s humiliation

parts.text: Ahaz worships Baalim, burns his children in the fire, and sacrifices throughout the land. God gives Judah into Syrian and Israelite hands, with heavy losses and many captives. Oded rebukes Israel for excessive fury and for intending to enslave their brethren, reminding them of their own guilt. Leaders heed him, and the captives are clothed, fed, cared for, and returned to Jericho.

As Edom and the Philistines also attack, Ahaz buys Assyrian help with sacred and royal treasures, but gains distress instead. He becomes more unfaithful, sacrificing to Damascus’s gods, damaging temple vessels, closing the temple, and multiplying altars. He dies without burial among the kings, and Hezekiah succeeds him.

chapters.title: Hezekiah reopens and cleanses the temple

parts.text: Hezekiah begins his reign by reopening and repairing the temple. He summons the priests and Levites to sanctify themselves and remove its uncleanness, acknowledging that their fathers’ neglect and unfaithfulness brought judgment. He intends to renew the covenant with God. The Levites cleanse the sanctuary and its vessels, including what Ahaz discarded, and report the work completed.

Hezekiah gathers the rulers for sacrifices and atonement for all Israel. Music and praise accompany the burnt offering, and the congregation worships and brings willing gifts. Levites assist because too few priests have yet sanctified themselves. Temple service is restored, and king and people rejoice that God has prepared them for this sudden renewal.

chapters.title: Israel is invited to keep the passover

parts.text: Hezekiah invites Judah and the northern tribes to celebrate passover in Jerusalem. It is held in the second month because the priests and people were not ready at the usual time. The messengers urge Israel to return to the merciful God of their fathers. Many mock them, but some humble themselves and come, while God gives Judah a united heart.

The assembly removes false altars and keeps the feast. When many eat without the required purification, Hezekiah prays for those whose hearts seek God, and the LORD hears and heals them. Worship and rejoicing continue for an additional seven days, with abundant royal gifts. The priests bless the people, and their prayer reaches heaven.

chapters.title: Provision for priests and Levites

parts.text: After the feast, the people destroy idols, groves, high places, and altars in Judah and parts of Israel. Hezekiah organizes priests and Levites for their appointed service and supplies the king’s portion for offerings. He commands support for those serving in God’s house. The people bring firstfruits and tithes so abundantly that large heaps accumulate, and the priests testify that God has blessed them.

Storerooms and responsible overseers are appointed to receive and distribute the gifts faithfully. Provision reaches the priests, Levites, and their households according to their service and genealogies, including those outside Jerusalem. Hezekiah’s work is described as wholehearted, good, right, and prosperous before God.

chapters.title: Assyria is defeated and Hezekiah is tested

parts.text: As Sennacherib invades, Hezekiah strengthens Jerusalem’s defenses and restricts outside water supplies. He encourages the people to trust God rather than fear human strength. Assyrian messengers mock that confidence and insult the LORD. Hezekiah and Isaiah pray, and God sends an angel to destroy Assyria’s warriors and commanders. Sennacherib returns home in shame and is later killed by his own sons.

Hezekiah receives help in mortal sickness but responds with pride, bringing wrath. He and Jerusalem humble themselves, delaying judgment. His wealth, building, and waterworks are described. During the Babylonian embassy, God leaves him to test what is in his heart. He dies honored, and Manasseh succeeds him.

chapters.title: Manasseh humbles himself; Amon does not

parts.text: Manasseh reverses Hezekiah’s reforms, worships the host of heaven, practices forbidden spiritual arts, burns his children, and places idols in God’s house. Judah becomes more corrupt than the nations God expelled. When warnings are ignored, Assyrian commanders take Manasseh captive to Babylon. In affliction he humbles himself and prays; God hears him and restores his kingdom, and he acknowledges the LORD as God.

Manasseh strengthens Jerusalem, removes foreign gods, repairs the altar, and commands Judah to serve the LORD, though worship at high places continues. His son Amon follows the earlier idolatry but does not humble himself. Servants kill Amon, and the people execute the conspirators and make Josiah king.

chapters.title: Josiah reforms worship and hears the law

parts.text: Josiah begins seeking God while young and purges Judah and Israel of idols and unlawful altars. During temple repairs, Hilkiah finds the book of the law given through Moses. Shaphan reads it to the king. Distressed by the people’s disobedience and the wrath it deserves, Josiah tears his clothes and sends to inquire of the LORD.

Huldah confirms that the written judgments will come because the people forsook God, but Josiah’s humility means he will not witness the coming disaster. He gathers the people, reads the covenant, and pledges wholehearted obedience. The assembly joins him, and he removes remaining abominations. Throughout his days they continue following the LORD.

chapters.title: Josiah’s passover and death at Megiddo

parts.text: Josiah holds a great passover in Jerusalem, organizing priests and Levites according to Moses’ law and the arrangements of David and Solomon. The king and leaders provide abundant animals. The Levites prepare the offerings and also serve the priests, singers, and gatekeepers so each can perform his duty. The celebration is described as unequaled since Samuel’s days.

Later, Josiah opposes Necho of Egypt on his way to war. Necho warns that God has sent him and tells Josiah not to interfere. Josiah disregards the warning, disguises himself, and fights at Megiddo. Wounded by archers, he is taken to Jerusalem and dies. Judah mourns deeply, and Jeremiah laments for him.

chapters.title: Jerusalem falls, and Cyrus permits a return

parts.text: Judah’s final kings fall under foreign control. Egypt removes Jehoahaz and installs Jehoiakim; Babylon later takes royal and temple treasures and carries Jehoiachin away. Zedekiah refuses Jeremiah’s warning and rebels against Nebuchadnezzar. Priests and people multiply their sins, despising God’s compassionate messengers until no remedy remains.

The Chaldeans kill the people, plunder and burn the temple, destroy Jerusalem’s walls and palaces, and deport the survivors. The land lies desolate and enjoys its sabbaths, fulfilling Jeremiah’s word concerning seventy years. At last God stirs Cyrus of Persia to proclaim that the LORD has charged him to build the temple. He permits God’s people to go up to Jerusalem.
